solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Ring and chatter excitedly, wanting king to lead dangerous expedition

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so a letter goes missing from the word it follows
something done excitedly is agitated and jumbled, so the letters are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: to ring is to sound a bell; the noun bell stands in
taken as written before losing a letter
R, from Rex, is the abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: Someone babbling nervously with no monarch to head a risky mission.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' looks like a phone call but gives the noun bell; R stands for Rex, Latin for king.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom comes from the fable of mice wanting a bell on the cat: it means taking on a risky task for the group.

clue.text: Badenoch initially remains in party

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is used

blocks.note: the opening letter of the surname
ash is what remains after burning

explanation.surface: Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, at first stays in her party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' looks political, given Badenoch, but it means a celebration.
explanation.definitionFit: A bash is informal slang for a lively social gathering or celebration.

clue.text: New title about medic provided theme

indicators.note: making something new means remaking it, so the letters are rearranged
about means surrounding, so one piece is wrapped round another

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
MO is a medical officer, a doctor
if means provided that

explanation.surface: A doctor's new job title came with a theme attached.
explanation.walkthrough: MO, medical officer, is a common crossword doctor; the rearranged title wraps round it before 'provided' is added.
explanation.definitionFit: A leitmotif is a recurring musical or literary idea, a central recurring theme of a work.

clue.text: Animal in children’s game here, having shed its skin

indicators.note: shedding a skin removes the outside, so only the inner letters of the word stay

blocks.note: tig is the British name for the chasing game also called tag
the inner two letters of the word

explanation.surface: A snake in a playground game sloughs its skin.
explanation.walkthrough: Tig is the British playground chasing game known elsewhere as tag; 'here' without its outer letters gives ER.
explanation.definitionFit: The tiger is a large striped big cat, one example of an animal.

clue.text: Just this Roman and others around

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: hic is Latin for this, the word a Roman would use
et al. is the Latin abbreviation for and others

explanation.surface: Only this one Roman and his companions are nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just' reads as 'only' but is the definition meaning fair; 'this Roman' asks for the Latin word.
explanation.definitionFit: A just person acts fairly and rightly, which is to behave in a morally sound, principled way.

clue.text: Stuffy, as bald Cockney might be

indicators.note: a Cockney speaker famously drops the opening aitch of a word, so that letter is lost

blocks.note: bald means having no hair

explanation.surface: A hot room is described the way a hairless Londoner might say it.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney is the East London accent known for dropping H at the start of words, so HAIRLESS loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A stuffy room lacks fresh ventilation, so it has no circulating oxygen to breathe.

clue.text: Barman at first had cider and beer sent over

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letters of the words that follow
sending something over turns it back the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the opening letter of each of these four words

explanation.surface: A pub barman starts by having cider, then beer is delivered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barman' looks like a pub worker, but it is a composer who writes music in bars.
explanation.definitionFit: Johann Sebastian Bach composed music written in measures called bars, so he is jokingly a man of bars.

clue.text: Going strong, boxer versus European

blocks.note: Muhammad Ali, the famous heavyweight
v is the abbreviation for versus
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A boxer still fighting fit against a European opponent.
explanation.walkthrough: The usual boxer in crosswords is Muhammad Ali.
explanation.definitionFit: Something still going strong remains active and thriving, which is a figurative sense of being alive.

clue.text: Leader, powerful and stubborn

blocks.note: a head is the leader of an organisation
a direct synonym

explanation.surface: A description of a forceful, obstinate boss.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a list of three qualities, but the first two build the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A headstrong person insists on their own way and refuses advice, the same as being obstinate.

clue.text: Police leader? Smart!

blocks.note: first meaning: the singer who fronted the band The Police
second meaning: to feel a sharp, burning pain

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a chief constable, but The Police is the rock band; smart is the verb for hurting sharply.
explanation.definitionFit: The singer Sting led the band The Police, and a wound that smarts stings with sharp pain.

clue.text: Note producer upset Chairman Mao in the end

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that letter is used
to upset something is to knock it over into disorder, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written
the final letter of the name

explanation.surface: Someone writes a memo that ends up annoying Chairman Mao.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note producer' suggests someone writing memos; here a note is a musical sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A harmonica is a mouth organ, an instrument that produces musical tones when blown.

clue.text: Busy seafront – he goes to hide

indicators.note: to hide is to conceal, so the letters sit concealed inside the words given

blocks.note: letters running across the three words

explanation.surface: A crowded promenade where a man goes looking for somewhere to hide.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs from the end of seafront through he into goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone on the go is constantly active and occupied, with no time to rest.

clue.text: Wonder biofuel – car I manufactured has it in back

indicators.note: to have something in is to hold it inside, so the letters sit concealed within the words
back means backwards, so the concealed letters are read from right to left

blocks.note: letters running across the four words, from the end of the first into the start of the last

explanation.surface: A wonder biofuel: a car I built runs on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manufactured' looks like an anagram signal and 'biofuel' like a word to define, but both only house the letters, read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A wonder is an amazing, inexplicable event, often attributed to divine intervention.

clue.text: Something of a shock?

blocks.note: surface reading: a jolt or fright, or an electrical jolt
setter's reading: a shock of hair is a thick mass, and one lock of it is part of that

explanation.walkthrough: A shock is also a thick bushy head of hair; 'something of' asks for a piece of it, a single lock.
explanation.definitionFit: A tress is a long lock of hair, which is one part of a dense mop or shock.

clue.text: Psychiatrists and believers accepting punishment

indicators.note: to accept is to take something in, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: theists believe in God
to take the rap is to take punishment

explanation.surface: Mental-health doctors and the faithful both agree to be punished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' is not a joining of two definitions: the definition is the first word only.
explanation.definitionFit: Psychiatrists treat mental illness, a kind of clinical role broadly covered by therapists.

clue.text: Spooner’s destiny: coastal city that’s horrible

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts are exchanged

blocks.note: destiny is FATE and the coastal city is HULL; swap their opening sounds

explanation.surface: A gloomy prophecy that a seaside city is ghastly.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the first sounds of FATE HULL gives HATE FULL. Hull is a port city in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Something hateful arouses loathing, as a horrible thing is detestable and unpleasant.

clue.text: Worries over wife cut by a sharp tool

indicators.note: a thing cut by another is split open with something pushed into the gap

blocks.note: to fret is to worry
taken as written
W is the abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: Someone frets about a wife being hurt by a blade.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' puts FRETS on top; FRETS plus W is then split by A.
explanation.definitionFit: A fretsaw is a fine-bladed saw for cutting intricate shapes, a cutting implement with teeth.

clue.text: Officer housed by fine homeless charity

indicators.note: something housed is kept inside a building, so one piece lives inside another

blocks.note: sheer fabric is fine and thin
Lt is the abbreviation for lieutenant

explanation.surface: A military officer given a roof by a good charity for the homeless.
explanation.walkthrough: Shelter is a British housing and homelessness charity; 'fine' means thin, as sheer stockings are.
explanation.definitionFit: Shelter is the name of a well-known UK organisation campaigning against homelessness and bad housing.

clue.text: Everything extremely suspect in Conservative lie

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes, the outermost letters of the word
in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: a direct synonym
the first and last letters of the word
a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: Everything about a Tory falsehood seems highly suspicious.
explanation.walkthrough: The two short pieces go in together, after the first letter of the party name.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall story is an exaggerated, implausible account, an untruth nobody should believe.

clue.text: Runs free, strangely, before quiet jog

indicators.note: strangely means in an odd way, so the letters appear in an unusual order

blocks.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
taken as written, to be rearranged
sh is the call for quiet

explanation.surface: A runner goes off oddly free before a gentle trot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jog' looks like light running, but here it is the verb as in jogging the memory.
explanation.definitionFit: To jog someone's memory is to prompt recall, which is what refreshing a memory does.

clue.text: Hot stream disturbed small creature

indicators.note: something disturbed is thrown out of order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: H is the abbreviation for hot on a tap
taken as written

explanation.surface: A hot spring disturbing some little animal.
explanation.walkthrough: H for hot joins the six letters of the second word before the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A hamster is a little rodent commonly kept as a pet, so it is a small animal.

clue.text: Like sheep, say, with rings, lines and, alternately, reins

indicators.note: alternately means every other one, so only alternate letters of the word are kept

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for with
two rings are two O shapes
L is the abbreviation for line, doubled for the plural
the second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: Farm animals kitted out with rings, ropes and reins.
explanation.walkthrough: Plurals here are doubled single letters: two O's for rings, two L's for lines.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheep are covered in fleece, so they are made of wool, and 'say' marks this as an example.

clue.text: Article stops unusual growth for animal

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the normal order, so the letters are rearranged
a stopper is plugged into an opening, so one piece is pushed into another

blocks.note: a is the indefinite article
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A newspaper article halts a strange lump growing on an animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Growth' looks like a synonym for a wart, but it is the letters to rearrange, with A dropped inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The warthog is a wild African pig with facial bumps, one example of a beast.

clue.text: Old people snap tigers on vacation

indicators.note: vacating a place empties it, so the word loses everything but its outer letters

blocks.note: a snap is a photograph, a pic
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Pensioners photographing big cats while on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old people' suggests pensioners, but it means an ancient people; 'on vacation' empties a word, not a holiday.
explanation.definitionFit: The Picts were an ancient tribe in northern Scotland, a people of the distant past.

clue.text: Near dead-end road

blocks.note: first meaning: nearby, not far away
second meaning: a residential street with no through access

explanation.walkthrough: The two senses are pronounced differently: an adjective with a soft S and a noun naming a street.
explanation.definitionFit: Close means nearby in space, and in Britain a close is a cul-de-sac street with one entrance.

clue.text: Damage non-electronic car parts? They suffer greatly

indicators.note: non- means without, so the letter it attaches to is taken away

blocks.note: to mar is to spoil or damage
tyres are parts of a car
E is the abbreviation for electronic, as in e-mail

explanation.surface: Vandalising old-fashioned, non-digital car components, and the victims suffer.
explanation.walkthrough: TYRES loses its E; British spelling of tyres is needed here.
explanation.definitionFit: A martyr endures severe pain or persecution, often for a cause, so such people endure terrible hardship.

clue.text: Poet turning tail, finding cause of ferment

indicators.note: a tail is the end, and turning it round makes just the final pair of letters swap direction

blocks.note: W. B. Yeats, the Irish poet

explanation.surface: A poet turns tail and finds the source of unrest.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the last two letters, the tail, turn round, so YEATS becomes YEAST.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeast is a fungus that converts sugar into alcohol and gas, driving fermentation in brewing and baking.

clue.text: Drove that woman mad at last

indicators.note: at last points to the end, so only the final letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: her refers to a woman
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone finally drove her crazy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drove' looks like the past tense of drive, but it is a noun: a group of animals moved together.
explanation.definitionFit: A drove is a flock of cattle or sheep being driven together, the same as a group of livestock.

clue.text: One times spinner cutting sample of fabric

indicators.note: a thing cutting into another goes inside it, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: a swatch is a small cloth sample
a top is a toy that spins

explanation.surface: Someone multiplying by one while a spinner slices a fabric sample.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One times' reads as multiplication but means a device that times things.
explanation.definitionFit: A stopwatch measures elapsed intervals precisely, so it is a device used to time events.

clue.text: All-rounder regularly dismissed without help

indicators.note: throwing out at regular intervals leaves every other letter of the word

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters

explanation.surface: A cricket all-rounder keeps getting out with no support from teammates.
explanation.walkthrough: An all-rounder is a cricketer who both bats and bowls, and dismissed suggests getting out.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something on one's own means unaided, by oneself with nobody assisting.

clue.text: Woman, Sprat, ultimately getting fat

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the word is used

blocks.note: a woman's name
the final letter of the name

explanation.surface: Jack Sprat's wife from the nursery rhyme, the one who could eat no lean, finally grows plump.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme has Jack Sprat eating no fat and his wife no lean, which makes fat fit the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Suet is the hard animal fat from around kidneys, used in British puddings and pastry.

clue.text: Eighty red fans going after black – that’s keen

indicators.note: fanning spreads things out and scatters them, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for black on pencils
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Eighty supporters in red chasing a rival team in black, all very enthusiastic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fans' looks like supporters but is a verb, spreading the letters out; B goes first because the anagram comes after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone bright-eyed is alert and eager, full of enthusiasm and energy.
